claims.claim: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments required areas failing ground-level ozone standards to use reformulated gasoline with increased oxygenate content.
claims.episode_span: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments directed the Environmental Protection Agency to require oxygenated gasoline in regions that failed to meet ozone standards.
claims.source_title: Fact Sheet | A Brief History of Octane in Gasoline: From Lead to Ethanol | EESI
claims.supporting_quote: The Clean Air Act Amendments (CAAA) of 1990 were the next major regulation of fuels. Among other things, CAAA requires areas that do not meet ground-level ozone standards to use reformulated gasoline (RFG). RFG has an increased oxygenate content, which helps it burn more completely.

claims.claim: The first phase of the federal reformulated gasoline program began in 1995.
claims.episode_span: Implementation moved quickly once the reformulated gasoline program began in 1995.
claims.supporting_quote: The reformulated gasoline program was mandated by Congress in the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments. The CAA intended that RFG would be blended to burn more cleanly than conventional gasoline and would reduce emissions of smog-forming and toxic pollutants. The first phase of the RFG program began in 1995

claims.claim: Between February and October 1996, Santa Monica shut down seven of its eleven water wells because of MTBE contamination; those wells had supplied about half the city's daily water demand.
claims.episode_span: The first documented municipal-well closures occurred in Santa Monica in 1996, when seven wells serving 45,000 people were shut down after MTBE concentrations exceeded state taste-and-odor thresholds.
claims.source_title: Statement of Craig Perkins, City of Santa Monica, on MTBE Water Pollution, December 9, 1997 (U.S. Senate EPW)
claims.supporting_quote: Between February and October of 1996, we shut down seven of the City's eleven water wells at two separate well fields because of the contamination. These wells had represented 71% of our local water well production and supplied about one half of Santa Monica's total daily water demand.

claims.claim: MTBE's high water solubility lets it spread through groundwater more easily than other gasoline components.
claims.episode_span: A handful of hydrologists and state health officials noted MTBE’s high water solubility and resistance to biodegradation in the early 1990s
claims.supporting_quote: MTBE spreads more easily underground than other gasoline components due to its higher solubility in water.

claims.claim: MTBE dissolves readily in groundwater and travels farther and faster than benzene and other gasoline hydrocarbons.
claims.episode_span: MTBE’s molecular structure allowed it to dissolve quickly in groundwater and travel farther and faster than the benzene or other hydrocarbons it was meant to replace.
claims.supporting_quote: MTBE spreads more easily underground than other gasoline components due to its higher solubility in water.

claims.claim: California regulation prohibited MTBE in California gasoline starting December 31, 2003 (i.e., the ban was in force from the start of 2004).
claims.episode_span: California banned MTBE in gasoline effective 2004, and most other states followed with phase-outs or outright prohibitions by 2006.
claims.source_title: Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 13, § 2262.6 - Prohibition of MTBE and Oxygenates Other than Ethanol in California Gasoline Starting December 31, 2003 | LII
claims.supporting_quote: Starting December 31, 2003, no person shall sell, offer for sale, supply or offer for supply California gasoline which has been produced at a California production facility in part by either (i) adding at the California production facility any methyl tertiary-butyl ether (MTBE) in neat form

claims.claim: Estimates for removing MTBE from U.S. groundwater and soil ranged from $1 billion to $30 billion.
claims.episode_span: Cleanup costs for MTBE sites have exceeded several billion dollars nationwide, with estimates for California alone running above $1 billion by the mid-2010s.
claims.supporting_quote: MTBE removal from groundwater and soil contamination in the U.S. was estimated to cost from $1 billion [ 40 ] to US$30 billion , [ 41 ] including removing the compound from aquifers and municipal water supplies and replacing leaky underground oil tanks.

claims.claim: State litigation over MTBE produced large awards, including a 2013 jury award of $236 million to New Hampshire to treat MTBE-contaminated groundwater.
claims.episode_span: Some states pursued litigation against refiners under product-liability theories, resulting in large settlements that funded treatment but did not restore lost aquifers.
claims.supporting_quote: In 2013 a jury awarded the State of New Hampshire $236 million in damages in order to treat groundwater contaminated by MTBE.

claims.claim: The Energy Policy Act of 2005 removed the oxygenate requirement for reformulated gasoline, and its lack of MTBE liability protection prompted refiners to substitute ethanol for MTBE.
claims.episode_span: Refiners shifted to ethanol, which carried its own infrastructure challenges including pipeline incompatibility and higher volatility.
claims.supporting_quote: The federal Energy Policy Act of 2005 removed the oxygenate requirement for reformulated gasoline and established a renewable fuel standard. [ 30 ] The lack of MTBE liability protection in the law also prompted refiners to substitute ethanol for MTBE as a gasoline additive.

claims.claim: MTBE became the dominant RFG oxygenate, used in 87 percent of reformulated gasoline by the late 1990s (RFG itself being roughly 30 percent of U.S. gasoline).
claims.episode_span: By 1995 roughly one-third of the nation’s gasoline contained MTBE, with the highest concentrations in California, New York, and New Jersey.
claims.source_title: Fact Sheet | A Brief History of Octane in Gasoline: From Lead to Ethanol | EESI
claims.supporting_quote: by the late 1990s, a petroleum product, methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), was used in 87 percent of RFG due to its ease of transport and blending.

claims.claim: Congress added Subtitle I to the Solid Waste Disposal Act in 1984, creating the federal program regulating underground storage tanks to minimize tank leaks.
claims.episode_span: underground storage tanks were already being upgraded under separate 1984 legislation, so officials assumed any leaks would be caught before widespread migration occurred
claims.source_title: Learn About Underground Storage Tanks (USTs) | US EPA
claims.supporting_quote: Subtitle I was added to the Solid Waste Disposal Act through the Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments. Created a federal program to regulate USTs containing petroleum and hazardous chemicals to limit corrosion and structural defects and thus minimize future tank leaks.
